claims.claim: Le Guin says that in describing an invented world you have to leave out an enormous amount, and that the leaving-out is half the art.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Plotz, 'The Story's Where I Go', Public Books, 15 June 2015
claims.quote: the leaving-out is half the art
claims.page: section I, 'Names Come First with Me'

claims.claim: Le Guin says that with an invented world you have to describe more than a realist does.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Plotz, 'The Story's Where I Go', Public Books, 15 June 2015
claims.quote: you have to describe more than a realist does
claims.page: section I, 'Names Come First with Me'

claims.claim: Le Guin praises Tolkien for telling the reader where they are and what the weather is and leaving the rest up to the reader.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Plotz, 'The Story's Where I Go', Public Books, 15 June 2015
claims.quote: You know where you are, you know what the weather is
claims.page: section I, 'Names Come First with Me'

claims.claim: Le Guin says names come first with her and that she cannot write about a character who does not have the right name.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by John Plotz, 'The Story's Where I Go', Public Books, 15 June 2015
claims.page: section I, 'Names Come First with Me'

claims.claim: Le Guin says Angelica Gorodischer's Kalpa Imperial is written in very simple, pure Spanish because the pieces are storyteller's stories.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interviewed by Euan Monaghan, Literary Hub, 1 April 2016
claims.quote: very simple, pure Spanish, because they’re storyteller’s stories

claims.claim: Le Guin describes her story 'The Matter of Seggri' as a compendium of reports on a world written by various observers over many years, taken from the archives of the Historians of Hain.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Foreword to The Birthday of the World
claims.quote: a compendium of reports on the society of a world
claims.page: foreword, paragraph on 'The Matter of Seggri'

claims.claim: Le Guin says the history of her invented Hainish universe consists largely of gaps.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Foreword to The Birthday of the World
claims.quote: its history consists largely of gaps

claims.claim: Le Guin argues that a book of stories linked by place, characters, theme and movement is a real form, which she proposes calling a story suite.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Foreword to The Birthday of the World
claims.quote: linked by place, characters, theme, and movement
claims.page: foreword, paragraph on Four Ways to Forgiveness

claims.feature: other: meaning is not a message
claims.claim: Le Guin says the meaning of a story may lie in the language itself and in the movement of the story as read, rather than in a tidy bit of advice.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'A Message About Messages', first published by CBC Magazine, 2005
claims.quote: in the language itself, in the movement of the story as read

claims.claim: Le Guin says a fantastic setting requires vivid and specific description, and that while characters may lose touch with their reality the storyteller cannot.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 95, 'Are they going to say this is fantasy?', 2 March 2015
claims.quote: A fantastic setting requires vivid and specific description

claims.claim: Le Guin says a toneless, inexact language is incapable of creating landscape, meaningful relationship or credible event.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 95, 'Are they going to say this is fantasy?', 2 March 2015
claims.quote: A toneless, inexact language is incapable of creating landscape

claims.claim: Le Guin says the imaginary must be imagined accurately and with scrupulous consistency.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 95, 'Are they going to say this is fantasy?', 2 March 2015

claims.claim: Le Guin says a generic landscape and vague perceptions must be brought to life by the language of the telling, since the whole thing is made out of words.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 95, 'Are they going to say this is fantasy?', 2 March 2015
claims.quote: must be brought to life by the language of the telling

claims.claim: Le Guin names as a fault of The Buried Giant that a character never once forgets to address his wife as 'princess', and says she came to wish he would.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 95, 'Are they going to say this is fantasy?', 2 March 2015
claims.quote: forgets to address his wife as “princess”

claims.claim: Le Guin praises William Alexander's Goblin Secrets for the unlabored imaginative authority and completeness of its setting and for the fine, vivid English it is written in.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 52, 'Some Recent Fantasies', 21 May 2012
claims.quote: unlabored imaginative authority and completeness of its setting

verdicts.trueWording: Of course, you have to leave out an enormous amount, too, and the leaving-out is half the art.
verdicts.note: Public Books interview fetched raw (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200). Section I 'Names Come First with Me'. Full sentence on page: 'With an invented world, though, you have to describe more than a realist does. Of course, you have to leave out an enormous amount, too, and the leaving-out is half the art.' Quote string is character-exact; both limbs (invented world; leaving-out is half the art) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: With an invented world, though, you have to describe more than a realist does.
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section I. Quote character-exact within that sentence; the claim adds nothing beyond it.

verdicts.trueWording: You know where you are, you know what the weather is, from what direction the wind's blowing.
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section I. Context: 'Tolkien is really such a master there. You know where you are, you know what the weather is, from what direction the wind's blowing. He tells you what he can about it - but the rest of it's up to you.' Praise of Tolkien, the weather limb and the rest-is-up-to-the-reader limb all present.

verdicts.trueWording: Names come first with me. I can't write about a character if he or she doesn't have a name. The right name.
verdicts.note: Same raw page, section I, in reply to Plotz's question about island names. Quote character-exact; the 'right name' limb is the next sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: those are in very simple, pure Spanish, because they're storyteller's stories
verdicts.note: Lit Hub page fetched raw (HTTP 200); byline 'Euan Monaghan', dated 'April 1, 2016' on the page. Full context: 'And my translation of Angelica Gorodischer, the Kalpa Imperial, I knew very little Spanish then, but those are in very simple, pure Spanish, because they're storyteller's stories, and I could work through them with the dictionary.' Quote character-exact.

verdicts.trueWording: 'The Matter of Seggri' is a compendium of reports on the society of a world called Seggri written by various observers over a period of many years.
verdicts.note: ursulakleguin.com foreword fetched raw (HTTP 200). Next sentence: 'These documents are from the archives of the Historians of Hain, who are to reports as squirrels are to nuts.' Every limb - various observers, many years, archives of the Historians of Hain - is on the page; quote character-exact.

verdicts.trueWording: Its Time Line is like something the kitten pulled out of the knitting basket, and its history consists largely of gaps.
verdicts.note:
Same raw foreword; verified it sits in body paragraph 2 by parsing the page's

elements, matching the cited page locator. Nuance recorded, not a deduction: on the page she reports that others call it 'the Hainish Universe' while she calls it the Ekumen - the referent of 'its' is that same invented universe, so the claim's wording is accurate.

verdicts.trueWording: a book of stories linked by place, characters, theme, and movement, so as to form, not a novel, but a whole
verdicts.note: Same raw foreword, paragraph on 'Old Music and the Slave Women' / Four Ways to Forgiveness. Later in the same paragraph: 'It is a real form, and deserves a real name. Maybe we could call it a story suite? I think I will.' Both the real-form limb and the proposed name are present; quote character-exact.

verdicts.trueWording: the meaning of the story might lie in the language itself, in the movement of the story as read, in an inexpressible sense of discovery, rather than a tidy bit of advice
verdicts.note: ursulakleguin.com 'A Message about Messages' fetched raw (HTTP 200); page footer confirms 'first published by CBC Magazine, 2005'. Quote character-exact. Framing nuance: Le Guin puts it as a rhetorical question to reviewers ('Does it ever occur to such reviewers that...'), which asserts the position rather than merely asking; 'may lie' in the claim tracks 'might lie' on the page, and the 'rather than a tidy bit of advice' limb is verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: A fantastic setting requires vivid and specific description; while characters may lose touch with their reality, the storyteller can't.
verdicts.note: ursulakleguin.com blog 95 fetched raw (HTTP 200), signed '- UKL 2 March 2015'. The sentence sits in body paragraph 3, matching the cited locator. Quote character-exact; both limbs are the two halves of one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: A toneless, inexact language is incapable of creating landscape, meaningful relationship, or credible event.
verdicts.note: Same raw blog 95 paragraph 3. Quote character-exact and the claim reproduces the whole sentence, including all three of landscape, meaningful relationship, credible event.

verdicts.trueWording: The imaginary must be imagined, accurately and with scrupulous consistency.

verdicts.trueWording: But so generic a landscape and such vague, elusive perceptions must be brought to life by the language of the telling. The whole thing is made out of words, after all.

verdicts.trueWording: how is it that Axl never, ever, not once, forgets to address his wife as “princess”? I came to wish very much that he would.
